1233.title: Jewish Renewal
1233.hook: Zalman Schachter-Shalomi joined Hasidic spirituality with egalitarian openness
1233.howItsDone: Jewish Renewal communities pray with chanting, wordless melodies, silence and movement alongside the traditional Hebrew service, and women and men lead prayer and serve as rabbis equally.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: many ways to picture God. Kaplan's God, a power in the world that makes for goodness. Today, a movement built around how people pray.

The chairs are in a circle, not rows. Someone starts a melody with no words, just a sound, and it goes around once, twice, ten times, until the whole room is carrying it. A woman leads the next prayer. A man near the window sways with his eyes closed. Then the room drops into a long silence before the Hebrew begins again. Some of this would be at home in a Hasidic study house; some would surprise the people praying there. The rabbi whose life made rooms like this possible was Zalman Schachter-Shalomi, called Reb Zalman by his students.
screen: `A CIRCLE OF CHAIRS.` → `A MELODY WITH NO WORDS.` → `THEN, SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Jewish Renewal. Roots first. Reb Zalman was formed in Hasidism, in the Chabad world, where prayer is meant to be felt as well as said: the wordless melody called a niggun, the joy, the long gathering around a rebbe's table. The Psalm says it plainly: "Serve the LORD with gladness: come before his presence with singing." Then the opening. He carried that warmth to people who would never have walked into a Hasidic synagogue, and in Renewal communities women and men lead prayer, teach and serve as rabbis side by side. Now the forms. Renewal gatherings may chant one line again and again until it settles, sit in silent meditation, move, sing in Hebrew and English, and pray with the body as well as the book. Reb Zalman cared about the craft of prayer the way a musician cares about practice: how to make the words land in a living person. Finally, the name. In the traditional service, as the Torah scroll goes back into the ark, the congregation sings a verse from Lamentations: "renew our days as of old." Renewal in that verse is not novelty. It is going back to a source to find it fresh. Other Jews ask real questions in return: how far new forms can stretch, and how binding halakha remains inside them. Renewal Jews hold a range of answers on that, too. The same verse is sung in Renewal circles and in Hasidic study houses, and each reads it in its own way.

segments.voice: Choose a single line and give it the whole sit. If you pray, take a line you already know, say "Serve the LORD with gladness," and repeat it slowly on the out-breath, quieter each time, until it is almost only breath; if you don't, hum one simple tune with no words, over and over. When your mind wanders, come back to the line or the tune; nobody is listening but you.
Jewish Renewal. The movement shaped by Reb Zalman Schachter-Shalomi: Hasidic warmth and prayer craft, opened to everyone, with women and men leading equally. Today's word.

1234.title: Humanistic Judaism
1234.hook: Sherwin Wine's Judaism of culture and ethics without theism
1234.howItsDone: Humanistic Jewish congregations celebrate the Jewish festivals and life-cycle events with ceremonies and readings centered on human history, culture and responsibility, without prayers addressed to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: renewal. Jewish Renewal carries Hasidic warmth and the craft of prayer to everyone. Today, a movement that keeps the people and its ethics, and sets theism aside.

Can a person be fully Jewish and not believe in God? You met that question on day one hundred fifty-four. Ask it around a Shabbat table and you may get a different answer from every chair. One says no, the covenant is with God. One says of course, look at my grandfather. One says it depends on what you mean by God. A rabbi in Michigan, Sherwin Wine, gave his answer by building something: a congregation that kept the holidays, the history, the Hebrew songs and the ethical demands of Jewish life, without addressing prayers to God. He called it Humanistic Judaism.
screen: `FULLY JEWISH, WITHOUT GOD?` → `AN ANSWER FROM EVERY CHAIR.` → `ONE RABBI BUILT HIS ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Humanistic Judaism. It began with one rabbi's honesty. Sherwin Wine decided he could not stand in front of a congregation and say words about God he did not believe. Rather than leave, he looked for a way to say only what he meant. Humanistic Judaism, as his movement describes itself, is a Judaism of culture and ethics without theism. What stays? The festivals stay: Passover, Hanukkah, the High Holy Days. Births, coming of age, weddings and funerals are marked with ceremony. The difference is in the words. Readings speak of human courage, human history and human responsibility, rather than praying to God. Where does the weight fall? On human hands. The Mishnah keeps a saying of Hillel: if I am not for myself, who will be for me; if I am only for myself, what am I; and if not now, when? In a Humanistic frame, that line carries the whole load: whatever good gets done in the world, people are the ones who do it. And there is honest disagreement. Jews in other movements push back, some strongly: for them, a Judaism without God leaves out the center, the One the Shema calls one. Humanistic Jews answer that a people, its memory and its ethics can also be a center. Both sides are describing their own Judaism, and neither needs the other as a foil. Some Jews say Jewish without theism, and they mean both halves of that sentence.

If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer, in your own words; if you don't, simply hold them in your attention, with respect. No arguing, no persuading, in either direction.

1235.title: Secular Jews
1235.hook: Yiddishists, Bundists, secular Israelis: Jewish through culture and people
1235.howItsDone: Secular Jews often express their Jewishness through language, literature, food, holidays kept as family and cultural occasions, community causes and connection to the Jewish people, without regular religious observance.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: Jewish without theism. Humanistic Judaism kept the festivals and ethics, and spoke of human hands. Today, Jews whose belonging runs through language and people more than prayer.

A weeknight in a Tel Aviv kitchen. The soup is on, a grandmother is arguing politics with her grandson, and everyone speaks Hebrew, the language of the prophets, about traffic. Rewind the tape and cross a continent. A meeting hall in a Polish city, a crowd singing labor songs in Yiddish, a school down the street teaching poetry and history in Yiddish too. Neither room has a prayer in it. Both are thick with Jewish life. Today's word names the people at home in rooms like these.
screen: `HEBREW, ABOUT TRAFFIC.` → `LABOR SONGS IN YIDDISH.` → `THICK WITH JEWISH LIFE.`

segments.voice: Secular Jews. Three groups and a book. The Yiddishists first. They held that Yiddish, the everyday language of Jews in Eastern Europe, could carry a whole modern culture: novels, theater, newspapers, schools. You did not need a synagogue to be Jewish. You needed a language and a people that spoke it. Then the Bundists. The Bund was a Jewish socialist movement, and its watchword was a Yiddish word, doikayt, hereness: build a just Jewish life right here, where we already live, in our own language. Other movements of that time gave other answers about where Jewish life should be built, and the arguments were fierce. Much of the world the Bund and the Yiddishists built was destroyed in the Holocaust. What they asked survives. Then secular Israelis. For some, Hebrew is simply the language of the morning bus, the Bible is read in school as the people's story and literature, and Shabbat is the day the family gathers, whether or not anyone lights a candle. And a thread inside the Bible itself. The book of Esther, in its Hebrew text, never names God. The people act. Mordecai tells Esther that if she stays silent, help will come from another place, then asks: "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" Rabbinic tradition reads God's hidden hand in that story, and the scroll is read aloud at Purim. A secular Jew may read the same verse as a call to act for one's people. Same scroll, two readings, and the people in the room are all Jews.

1236.title: The Karaites today
1236.hook: a small community still keeps the written Torah without the rabbinic tradition
1236.howItsDone: Karaite Jews keep the commandments of the Hebrew Bible as they read them directly, set their calendar by the new moon and the ripening barley, and pray in their own synagogues, including full prostration.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: secular and Jewish. Yiddishists, Bundists and secular Israelis belong through language, culture and people. Today, a community whose way runs through the written text alone.

Late winter, a field of young barley. A few people walk the rows, stopping to bend down and rub the heads of grain between their fingers. Are they ripe enough? It matters, because for this community the answer helps decide when the new year of months begins, and so when Passover falls. The Torah calls that season Abib, and they go out to look for it in the field itself. These are Karaite Jews, a small community that has kept its own path for a very long time.
screen: `A FIELD OF YOUNG BARLEY.` → `IS IT RIPE?` → `PASSOVER WAITS ON THE FIELD.`

segments.voice: The Karaites today. The principle is simple. Karaites read the written Torah and the rest of the Hebrew Bible as the authority, without the Oral Torah that rabbinic Judaism holds alongside it, the tradition gathered in the Mishnah and the Talmud. They point to a verse in Deuteronomy: "Ye shall not add unto the word which I command you, neither shall ye diminish ought from it." Karaite tradition credits an early teacher with a line often paraphrased as: search the scripture well, and do not lean on my opinion. Each reader is responsible for reading. Here is what that looks like. The Torah says, "This day came ye out in the month Abib," so Karaites look to the ripening barley and the new moon for their calendar. And you met this verse with the Law Committee: "Ye shall kindle no fire throughout your habitations upon the sabbath day." Karaites have traditionally read it to mean no fire left burning on Shabbat, while rabbinic Jews read the same verse, with the Oral Torah, as allowing a light lit before Shabbat begins. Same verse, two readings. Karaite prayer also includes bowing down fully, the whole body to the ground. And the last word of today's title: today. Karaites are not a chapter in a history book. There are Karaite synagogues and families now, in Israel and elsewhere, keeping their festivals by the field and the moon. Rabbinic Jews and Karaites have argued long and hard, and this lesson need not settle it. It only needs to say the plain thing: a community that reads the Torah its own way is still here.

1237.title: Who is a Jew?
1237.hook: Orthodox and Conservative follow the mother's line; Reform and Reconstructionist also accept the father's, with upbringing
1237.howItsDone: Orthodox and Conservative communities count as Jewish a child of a Jewish mother or a convert; Reform and Reconstructionist communities also count a child of a Jewish father who is raised with Jewish identity and practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: still here. The Karaites keep the written Torah, by the barley and the moon, without the rabbinic tradition. Today, a question the streams answer differently.

Two cousins at a family wedding. Both grew up with Shabbat dinners at their grandmother's, both learned Hebrew, both had a bar or bat mitzvah. One cousin's mother is Jewish. The other cousin's father is Jewish, and his mother is not. At the reception someone asks, half joking, which of them the synagogue across town would count as Jewish. The table goes quiet. The honest reply is: it depends on which synagogue. You heard the short version on day forty-five. Today, the fuller one.
screen: `TWO COUSINS, ONE GRANDMOTHER.` → `MOTHER'S SIDE, FATHER'S SIDE.` → `IT DEPENDS WHICH SYNAGOGUE.`

segments.voice: Who is a Jew? The classic rule comes first. The Mishnah, in the tractate on marriage, teaches that when a Jewish father and a mother who is not Jewish have a child, the child follows the mother. The Talmud reads this out of a verse in Deuteronomy. In rabbinic law, then, Jewish status passes through the mother, and a person can also become Jewish by conversion, which is tomorrow's story. Orthodox and Conservative Judaism keep this rule. Now a surprise inside the rule: some things still pass through the father. In the Torah, the people are counted "after their families, by the house of their fathers," and to this day a kohen, a member of the priestly family, is a kohen because his father was. So even in traditional law, the mother's line and the father's line each carry something. Then the other answer. Reform and Reconstructionist Judaism also accept a child of a Jewish father, when the child is raised as a Jew and takes part in Jewish life. For them, a Jewish parent on either side opens the door, and the upbringing walks through it. And for real people: the two cousins may be welcomed in one synagogue and asked about their mother in another. Each stream is trying to be faithful to what it holds, and none needs to be painted as cruel or careless to explain itself. Different answers, given with conviction, and real families living right across the line between them.

1238.title: Conversion across streams
1238.hook: requirements differ, and not every stream recognizes every conversion
1238.howItsDone: People who convert to Judaism study with a rabbi and join a community; depending on the stream, conversion includes a beit din, immersion in a mikveh and, for men, circumcision, and the convert takes a Hebrew name.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: different answers. The mother's line for some streams, either parent with a Jewish upbringing for others. Today, the door that stands open to anyone: choosing.

"Thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." A young widow from Moab says it on a road, to her mother-in-law, who has just told her, again, to go home. Ruth does not go home. She walks into a people not her own, and the book that bears her name ends with a family tree: her great-grandson is King David. Tradition remembers her as someone who joined the Jewish people by choice. You met another, Ovadiah, on day forty-five. How that choosing works today is today's word.
screen: `A WIDOW ON THE ROAD.` → `THY PEOPLE SHALL BE MY PEOPLE.` → `HER GREAT-GRANDSON, DAVID.`

segments.voice: Conversion across streams. The old shape first. The Talmud describes someone who comes to convert. They are asked why, and told honestly that the Jewish people has known hardship. If they still say, I know, and I want this, they are taught some of the commandments, light ones and weighty ones, and welcomed. Now the steps today. In Orthodox and Conservative Judaism, conversion usually means a time of study, a court of three called a beit din, immersion in a mikveh, a ritual bath, and for men, circumcision. Reform and Reconstructionist rabbis also ask for study and commitment; how they handle immersion and circumcision varies from community to community. Then the hard part. Because the streams disagree about authority, not every stream recognizes every other stream's conversions. Orthodox courts, for instance, accept conversions done to Orthodox standards. A person can stand inside one community as a Jew and be asked questions in another. That is painful, and each stream would say it is guarding something it holds sacred, not shutting anyone out lightly. And the welcome. The Torah commands that the stranger who lives among you "shall be unto you as one born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself." The Talmud adds that you must never remind a convert of who they used to be. Once someone has come in, they are simply family. Requirements differ across the streams. The Torah's welcome stands in the scripture they share.

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who joined something by choice: a person who converted, a new citizen, someone who married into a family and learned its jokes, a newcomer at work. Conversion across streams. Joining the Jewish people by choice: requirements differ from stream to stream, and not every stream recognizes every conversion. Today's word.
Your line: many doors. Different requirements across the streams, and the same old welcome. Until tomorrow.

1239.title: Israeli categories
1239.hook: most Israelis describe themselves as secular, traditional, religious or Haredi
1239.howItsDone: Israeli Jews may describe themselves as hiloni (secular), masorti (traditional), dati (religious) or haredi, and these self-chosen words shape everyday conversation about schools, neighborhoods and Shabbat.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: many doors, and the Torah's welcome: as one born among you. This week ran through renewal, Jewish without theism, secular and Jewish, still here, different answers and many doors. Today it ends in Israel.

Ask an Israeli about religion, and the answer may not be the name of a movement at all. Often it is one of four Hebrew words. A taxi driver says one. The woman in the next seat on the bus says another. A soldier home for the weekend says a third, and the young man in the black coat at the corner says the fourth. Four words. They describe how a person lives. They are today's word.
screen: `NOT A MOVEMENT'S NAME.` →`FOUR HEBREW WORDS.` → `HOW A PERSON LIVES.`

segments.voice: Israeli categories. One word at a time. First, hiloni: secular. Some readers hear in it chol, the ordinary, the weekday, the opposite of holy. The Torah tells the priests to "put difference between holy and unholy," and in Hebrew that unholy is chol. As Shabbat ends, the Havdalah blessing praises God who separates holy from ordinary. A hiloni Israeli lives mostly on the ordinary side of that line, in Hebrew, with the Bible as the people's story, and may still light candles at Hanukkah or sit at a seder. Second, masorti: traditional, keeping what is handed down. A masorti Israeli keeps some of it, often Friday night and the festivals, without keeping all of it. Careful: Masorti is also the name of the Conservative movement in Israel, but as a word about yourself it simply means traditional. Tomorrow stays with this middle. Third, dati: religious. Some readers hear in it dat, the word the book of Esther uses for the king's law. A dati Israeli keeps halakha; some call themselves dati leumi, national religious, the Religious Zionists from earlier in this block. Fourth, haredi, the Haredi communities from earlier in the block; the name echoes Isaiah's words to those who tremble: "ye that tremble at his word." Here is the turn: these are words people choose for themselves, and they overlap. Someone can be hiloni and fast on Yom Kippur. Someone masorti can pray every morning. The lines are blurry because they describe lives, not membership cards.
screen: `HILONI: THE ORDINARY SIDE.` · `MASORTI: SOME OF WHAT'S HANDED DOWN.` · `DATI: KEEPING THE LAW.` · `WORDS PEOPLE CHOOSE FOR THEMSELVES.` · then, large: `HILONI, MASORTI, DATI.`

segments.voice: On each out-breath, say one word quietly: hiloni, and let the ordinary weekday come to mind; masorti, and something handed down to you; dati, someone who keeps a whole law with care; haredi, those who tremble at God's word. Go round again, slower, until the four words feel like four neighbors rather than four boxes. If you pray, you can hold all four in your prayer.

Israeli categories. Hiloni, secular; masorti, traditional; dati, religious; haredi, a name that echoes those who tremble at God's word: four words Israelis use to describe how they live. Today's word.
Your line: hiloni, masorti, dati. One word can carry a whole way of living. That's a week.
